summary: Describes a URN namespace for the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers, for naming persistent resources SMPTE produces or manages. A sub-namespace for Universal Labels is described. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives a movie and TV standards group its own official naming system, so their items have permanent names that work anywhere.

subtitle: Permanent names for resources from the motion picture and television engineering standards body.

tldr.problem: The Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE) needs a standard way to assign unique, permanent, location-independent names to resources it produces or manages, such as standards documents and Universal Labels used in media encoding.
tldr.mechanism: SMPTE registers a formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace with the IANA, defining the namespace ID 'smpte' and establishing rules for how identifiers within that namespace are structured, assigned, and resolved. A subnamespace for Universal Labels is specifically defined.
tldr.outcome: SMPTE and systems that work with SMPTE resources gain a standardized namespace for permanent identification. The URN namespace is registered with IANA and provides both human and automated access to SMPTE resources through online systems.

facts.label: Registrant
facts.value: Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers

today: RFC 5119 is not obsoleted or updated. The SMPTE URN namespace is registered with IANA and remains active. SMPTE resources, including standards documents and Universal Labels, are identified within this namespace. The SMPTE Registration Authority continues to maintain the metadata dictionary and registry at smpte-ra.org, providing resolution services for SMPTE URNs.

sections.title: SMPTE and Its Namespace Need
sections.content:
SMPTE (Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers) is an internationally-recognized standards-developing organization headquartered in the United States with members in over 80 countries. SMPTE develops Engineering Documents, including Standards, Recommended Practices, and Guidelines, through its Technology Committees. The organization also maintains the SMPTE Registration Authority, which registers Universal Labels (ULs) used to identify the type and encoding of data within audio-visual material.

SMPTE needs to assign unique, permanent, and location-independent names to the resources it produces or manages. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) provides exactly this capability: a persistent identifier that does not depend on where a resource is physically stored or how to access it. By registering a formal URN namespace, SMPTE ensures that its resources can be referenced consistently and reliably.
sections.plainLanguage: SMPTE makes standards for movies and TV. They manage a big registry of codes that label different types of video and audio data. They needed an official name system so these resources have permanent, unchanging names.

sections.title: Formal Namespace Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers a formal URN namespace according to RFC 3406. The namespace ID is smpte. All URNs in the namespace follow the structure defined in SMPTE 2029-2007 and conform to RFC 2141 (URN Syntax). The namespace specific string (NSS) of all SMPTE URNs follows this pattern: urn:smpte: followed by either a subnamespace identifier or other components.

SMPTE may add additional subnamespaces in the future. Systems working with SMPTE URNs should be designed with awareness that new subnamespaces could appear at any time. The RFC specifically defines the urn:smpte:ul: subnamespace for Universal Labels, which uses a syntax of colon-separated four-byte (8 hex digit) groups, for example: urn:smpte:ul:060E2B34.04010103.04010202.01011100.
sections.plainLanguage: SMPTE URNs all start with 'urn:smpte:'. The most common ones are Universal Labels, which look like codes made of hex digits and dots.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Persistence Guarantees
sections.content:
Identifier uniqueness: SMPTE 2029 specifies that all URNs in the SMPTE namespace shall not be re-assigned. URNs remain valid even if the owners or registrants of the resources are no longer members or customers of SMPTE. For Universal Labels specifically, the SMPTE-administered rules require that each UL be unique within the UL space and cannot be reassigned or reused. The RFC notes that SMPTE Universal Labels are 'object identifiers' as specified by ISO/IEC 8824-1, though the SMPTE representation carries additional semantics beyond a simple OID.

Identifier persistence: SMPTE-administered ULs may occasionally be deleted through SMPTE procedures, but even after deletion, a UL will not be reused. Revisions to a UL result in a new UL being created and the old one deleted. The persistence rules for future SMPTE subnamespaces will be defined in the SMPTE Standards that establish them.
sections.plainLanguage: Once SMPTE assigns a name to something, that name stays assigned forever. If something changes, they create a new name instead of reusing an old one. This means old names keep meaning what they originally meant.

sections.title: Assignment and Resolution Processes
sections.content:
Assignment: Assignment of URNs in the SMPTE namespace is limited to SMPTE and authorities specifically designated by SMPTE. Assignment follows SMPTE's due process procedures developed through its Technology Committees. Some Universal Label registrations may require a fee and supporting technical documentation. Applicants must provide their name and address; some label classes require submission of technical documentation and evaluation through the SMPTE Engineering Committee process.

Resolution: SMPTE-administered ULs are resolved through publications of the SMPTE Registration Authority, currently including the Metadata Dictionary (per SMPTE RP210) and the SMPTE Labels Registry (per SMPTE RP224), both available at http://www.smpte-ra.org/mdd/. SMPTE expects to develop and maintain URN catalogs that map all future assigned URNs to Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) to enable Web-based resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: Only SMPTE can assign official names in their namespace. When someone wants a name, they ask SMPTE with documentation. SMPTE keeps a registry online so you can look up any name to find what it refers to.

sections.title: Comparison and Equivalence Rules
sections.content:
Lexical equivalence rules determine when two URN strings refer to the same resource. For Universal Labels in the urn:smpte:ul subnamespace, lexical equivalence is defined by case-insensitive string comparison. This means urn:smpte:ul:060e2b34.04010103.04010202.01011100 and urn:smpte:ul:060E2B34.04010103.04010202.01011100 refer to the same resource, despite the uppercase and lowercase differences.

For other subnamespaces of urn:smpte:, lexical equivalence will be specified in the SMPTE document that defines each subnamespace. In the absence of specific rules, equivalence is defined by exact string match according to RFC 2141. This approach gives SMPTE flexibility to define different matching rules for different types of resources as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: For Universal Labels, capitalization does not matter—a name with uppercase letters is the same as the same name with lowercase letters. For other types of SMPTE names, the rules might be different.

sections.title: Security and Considerations
sections.content:
The SMPTE URN namespace shares the security considerations outlined in RFC 3406, which addresses URN namespace registration broadly. The RFC does not identify other known security considerations specific to SMPTE URNs. Because URNs are persistent identifiers (not resolved like URLs), they do not introduce the same risks as URLs that might resolve to malicious content.

The RFC notes that SMPTE is an internationally-recognized standards-developing organization, and the namespace provides a uniform and effective way for the motion imaging industry to communicate resource names. The namespace supports both human and automated access to SMPTE-managed resources through online systems.
sections.plainLanguage: There are not many security risks with a simple naming system like this. The main security considerations are the same for all URN namespaces: make sure you trust the organization managing the names.
